reviewPolicy: Compilation does not certify historical fidelity. Independent philosophical review is pending.

items.local: Two arbitrary things with nothing in common.
items.limit: Axiom V is interpreted as absence of conceptual dependence. This is an intermediate lemma, not a numbered proposition.
items.title: No conceptual dependence
items.formalStatement: If two things have nothing in common, neither is conceived through the other.
items.exactLean:
theorem conceptual_separation {Entity : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity)
    (a5 : Axiom5 v) (x y : Entity) (h : ¬ v.common x y) :
    ¬ v.depends x y ∧ ¬ v.depends y x

premises.title: Nothing in common
premises.interpretation: Formal convention: absence of commonality excludes conceptual dependence in both directions.

items.local: Two arbitrary things with nothing in common.
items.limit: Knowledge of a cause is represented by conceptual dependence. The logical implication is checked; this reading of knowledge still requires philosophical review.
items.title: No causation without commonality
items.formalStatement: Things with nothing in common cannot cause one another.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition3 {Entity : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity)
    (a4 : Axiom4 v) (a5 : Axiom5 v) (x y : Entity)
    (h : ¬ v.common x y) : ¬ v.causes x y ∧ ¬ v.causes y x

sourceStatement.en: Things which have nothing in common cannot be one the cause of the other.
sourceStatement.fr: Les choses qui n’ont rien de commun ne peuvent être causes l’une de l’autre.

items.local: A substance and a distinct proposed cause.
items.limit: The proof excludes the encoded causal relation. Production is not a separately formalized relation.
items.title: No external cause of substance
items.formalStatement: A substance cannot be produced by a cause external to itself, in the reconstructed causal vocabulary.
items.exactLean:
theorem external_cause_excluded {Entity : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity)
    (a4 : Axiom4 v) (s cause : Entity) (hs : Substance v s)
    (external : cause ≠ s) : ¬ v.causes cause s

items.local: The same cause and the same effect.
items.limit: A definitional consequence of the chosen adequate/partial cause encoding, not a numbered proposition.
items.title: An adequate cause is not partial
items.formalStatement: For the same effect, a cause cannot be both adequate and partial in this encoding.
items.exactLean:
theorem adequate_not_partial {Entity Event : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity Event)
    (x : Entity) (e : Event) (h : AdequateCause v x e) :
    ¬ PartialCause v x e

premises.title: Adequate and partial causes
premises.interpretation: Formal convention: adequacy includes causation and intelligibility through this cause alone. Partial causation includes causation and excludes that intelligibility.

items.local: The same actor and the same event.
items.limit: Excludes simultaneous activity and passivity only for this actor-event pair, not every combination of action and passion in a person.
items.title: Activity excludes passivity for this event
items.formalStatement: For one actor and one event, activity and passivity exclude one another in the reconstructed definitions.
items.exactLean:
theorem active_not_passive {Entity Event : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity Event)
    (x : Entity) (e : Event) (h : Active v x e) : ¬ Passive v x e

premises.title: Adequate and partial causes
premises.interpretation: Formal convention: adequacy includes causation and intelligibility through this cause alone. Partial causation includes causation and excludes that intelligibility.

premises.title: Activity and passivity
premises.interpretation: Formal convention: activity and passivity are relative to the same actor and event. This does not exclude a person being active in one respect and passive in another.

items.local: A substance and its distinct mode.
items.limit: Priority by nature is interpreted as asymmetric conceptual dependence. Other meanings of priority have not been proved equivalent.
items.title: Substance is prior to its modes
items.formalStatement: A mode depends conceptually on its substance; the substance does not depend on that distinct mode. This reconstructs priority as asymmetric conceptual dependence.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition1 {Entity : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity)
    (s m : Entity) (hs : Substance v s) (hm : ModeOf v m s) :
    ConceptuallyPrior v s m

sourceStatement.en: Substance is by nature prior to its modifications.
sourceStatement.fr: La substance est par nature antérieure à ses modifications.

premises.title: Modes of substance
premises.interpretation: Formal convention: ModeOf names a distinct entity in which the mode exists and on which its conception depends. Priority in Proposition I is reconstructed as asymmetric conceptual dependence, not temporal precedence.

items.limit: Uses the alternative corollary argument. The original proof through P2/P3/P5 and the broader notion of production remain unformalized.
items.title: Distinct substances cannot cause each other
items.formalStatement: In the causal encoding, neither of two distinct substances causes the other. This uses the corollary’s alternative argument, not Spinoza’s full historical proof of Proposition VI.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition6_causal {Entity : Type} (v : Vocabulary Entity)
    (a4 : Axiom4 v) (s t : Entity) (hs : Substance v s)
    (ht : Substance v t) (distinct : s ≠ t) :
    ¬ v.causes s t ∧ ¬ v.causes t s

sourceStatement.en: One substance cannot be produced by another substance.
sourceStatement.fr: Une substance ne peut être produite par une autre substance.

items.local: Two actually existing substances of the same nature.
items.limit: The general multiplicity principle is assumed, not proved. The theorem says nothing about sharing a single attribute. It uses the later scholium instead of the original demonstration.
items.textualNote: The Latin proof cites Definition III and Axiom VI here; the imported Elwes proof prints Definitions III and VI. The library preserves that edition. This reference difference must be resolved against the Latin before reconstructing the original proof.
items.title: Uniqueness within the same nature
items.formalStatement: Two existing substances of the same nature are identical, assuming the scholium’s multiplicity principle. This does not establish uniqueness from sharing only one attribute.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition5_same_nature {E : Type} (v : Vocabulary E)
    (a4 : Spinoza.Axiom4 v.toVocabulary) (multiplicity : MultiplicityExplanation v)
    (x y : E) (hx : v.actual x) (hy : v.actual y)
    (sx : Spinoza.Substance v.toVocabulary x)
    (_sy : Spinoza.Substance v.toVocabulary y) (same : v.sameNature x y) : x = y

sourceStatement.en: There cannot exist in the universe two or more substances having the same nature or attribute.
sourceStatement.fr: Il ne peut y avoir dans la nature deux ou plusieurs substances de même nature ou attribut.

items.local: A substance already assumed to exist actually.
items.limit: Essential existence remains a primitive predicate in this version. The intrinsic/external explanation alternative is assumed. No existing substance or God is thereby established.
items.title: Essential existence of an existing substance
items.formalStatement: An existing substance has essence involving existence, assuming the selected explanation principle. This does not prove that a substance exists.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition7_existing_substance {E : Type} (v : Vocabulary E)
    (a4 : Spinoza.Axiom4 v.toVocabulary) (explanation : ExistenceExplanation v)
    (x : E) (hx : v.actual x) (sx : Spinoza.Substance v.toVocabulary x) :
    SelfCaused v x

sourceStatement.en: Existence belongs to the nature of substances.
sourceStatement.fr: Il appartient à la nature de la substance d’exister.

premises.title: Essential self-causation
premises.interpretation: Essential self-causation is distinct from a thing causing itself in the causal relation. Actual existence is recorded separately.

items.local: A substance already assumed to exist actually.
items.limit: Only distinct actual same-nature limiters are excluded. Modal necessity is absent. The limiter classification is used by this proof route but is not a minimal logical requirement of the stronger multiplicity premise.
items.title: No same-nature limiter of substance
items.formalStatement: An existing substance has no distinct actual limiter of the same nature, under the selected multiplicity principle and limiter bridge. This is a limited sense of infinity, without modal necessity.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition8_no_limiter {E : Type} (v : Vocabulary E)
    (a4 : Spinoza.Axiom4 v.toVocabulary) (multiplicity : MultiplicityExplanation v)
    (limiter : SubstanceLimiter v) (x : E) (hx : v.actual x)
    (sx : Spinoza.Substance v.toVocabulary x) : InfiniteInKind v x

premises.title: Finitude in its kind
premises.interpretation: Limited reconstruction: a limiter is distinct and actually exists. Infinity in kind means absence of such a limiter; it is not cardinal infinity or modal necessity.

items.local: A substance and another substance whose essential aspects it includes.
items.limit: An intermediate lemma in the attribute vocabulary. Reality inclusion is defined on essential aspects. The selected representation principle connects perception to those aspects; completeness is not needed for this step.
items.title: Essential inclusion preserves attributes
items.formalStatement: If a substance includes all the essential aspects of another, it has all of its attributes under the selected representation principle.
items.exactLean:
theorem attributes_monotone {T A R C : Type} (v : Vocabulary T A R C)
    (representation : EssenceRepresentation v) (more less : T)
    (substance : Substance v more) (includes : RealityIncludes v more less) :
    ∀ a, AttributeOf v a less → AttributeOf v a more

premises.title: Attribute
premises.interpretation: The attribute vocabulary distinguishes perception, essential aspects and conceptual requirements. Definition IV alone does not identify these relations; the additional interpretations are separately selectable.

premises.title: Attributes represent essential aspects
premises.interpretation: Selected interpretation: each attribute expresses one aspect, and perception agrees with possession of that aspect. This is stronger than the primitive perception relation in Definition IV. More reality is interpreted as inclusion of essential aspects.

items.local: Two substances with strictly nested sets of essential aspects. Their existence is not established by this proof.
items.limit: Restricted to substances and a structural reading of more reality. Strict set inclusion does not imply greater infinite cardinality. Representation and coverage are explicit interpretive premises, not the historical proof established from Definition IV alone. This attribute vocabulary has not been identified with the older causal or modal vocabulary.
items.title: More essential aspects, an additional attribute
items.formalStatement: For two substances, strict inclusion of essential aspects implies strict inclusion of attributes, assuming representation and completeness. This is a structural reading of more reality, not a comparison of infinite cardinalities.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition9_attribute_inclusion {T A R C : Type} (v : Vocabulary T A R C)
    (representation : EssenceRepresentation v) (coverage : AttributeCoverage v)
    (more less : T) (hm : Substance v more) (_hl : Substance v less)
    (reality : MoreReality v more less) : MoreAttributes v more less

sourceStatement.en: The more reality or being a thing has, the greater the number of its attributes (Def. iv.).
sourceStatement.fr: Plus une chose possède de réalité ou d’être, plus il lui appartient d’attributs (définition IV).

premises.title: Every essential aspect has an attribute
premises.interpretation: Selected completeness premise, not a numbered axiom. No finiteness or one-to-one correspondence is assumed. A Lean countermodel shows that representation without completeness does not ensure an additional attribute.

items.local: An attribute perceived as constituting the essence of a substance.
items.limit: Conceived through itself means absence of external conceptual requirements in this vocabulary. Transferring a requirement from attribute to substance is an additional interpretation; a compiled countermodel shows that D3 and primitive D4 alone do not justify that transfer. The scholium is not formalized.
items.title: Attributes need no external concept
items.formalStatement: An attribute of a substance has no external conceptual requirement, assuming the selected transfer of requirements to that substance. This is the encoded reading of conceived through itself.
items.exactLean:
theorem proposition10_attribute_independence {T A R C : Type} (v : Vocabulary T A R C)
    (inheritance : ConceptualInheritance v) (s : T) (a : A)
    (ha : AttributeOf v a s) : ConceivedThroughItself v a

sourceStatement.en: Each particular attribute of the one substance must be conceived through itself.
sourceStatement.fr: Chaque attribut d’une même substance doit se concevoir par soi.

premises.title: Transfer of conceptual requirements
premises.interpretation: Selected interpretation of the step from Definition IV to Definition III in P10. External requirements are relative to each conception. Their transfer is assumed explicitly; it is not proved by the perception relation alone.
